newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - New Thai finance merger steps raise worries.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - New Thai finance merger steps raise worries.

text.p: Tough new Thai central bank measures to be implemented this week to fend off disaster in the frail finance sector will shake the troubled industry but were seen as a positive move, analysts said on Sunday.
The central bank has said it will force 16 ailing finance firms to merge with healthy ones.
Analysts likened the moves set on Friday, to an earthquake which will send aftershocks rippling through the sector.

"I think these moves could be quite positive in helping to restructure the industry in the longer term though in reality it is still likely to be a time consuming process," said Suraphol Thipvilai, assistant research manager at Vickers Ballas.

The Bank of Thailand held urgent meetings with finance institutions over the weekend to detail the workings of the latest steps and seek their cooperation to soften the impact on nervous local depositors and the sector as a whole.

The authorities assured depositors with the 16 firms that their money was intact. The depositors could transfer their promissory notes to Krungthai Thanakit Plc, a unit of state-run Krung Thai Bank Plc, effective on Monday.

Depositors with other finance firms in the 91-company sector also had the choice of moving their deposits to Krung Thai Bank if they were nervous about the health of the sector but they would not be able to redeem their money immediately.
The central bank said it would also place controls on deposit rates offered by finance firms on Monday, in a bid to ease the companies' cost burdens. No details were given.

"Depositors with the 16 finance firms have no choice but to turn to Krungthai Thanakit to protect their money. For others there is a choice but we don't see a big move from them out to Krung Thai this week," said a manager at a local finance firm.

Depositors who moved their money to the two financial institutions would get much lower interest rates than the double-digit figures offered in the past by finance companies scrambling to raise funds, said the manager who declined to be identified.
But foreign creditors of affected finance firms were on tenterhooks with the central bank yet to clarify the fate of foreign loans to the companies.

"Foreign bank creditors are sweating as they await more clearer details from the central bank on the fate of their money to the 16 affected finance firms," said Graham Catterwell, managing director of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Analysts said many foreign creditors of affected Thai finance firms had been calling the central bank for more information.
"Foreigners will be wary about lending in future to Thai institutions if they are not told precisely what will happen to their interests soon," Catterwell said.
The local finance firm manager said foreigners were the most exposed group to the 16 finance firms.
"The foreigners lent money to the firms under free market rules and now if they want to recover it looks as if they have no choice but to seek legal recourse," he added.
The crisis-ridden Thai finance sector has been hit by overexposure to the depressed property sector.
High interest rates have caused a severe liquidity crunch in the sector and the country's worst economic downturn in over a decade has hurt business badly.

Finance firm stocks have been dumped as a result of doubts over the quality of their assets and their non-performing loans. Their demise has badly dented the Thai stock index which has recently been lingering near eight year lows.
Analysts said the new finance measures were unlikely to affect the baht, but if implementation of the steps ran into snags, then speculators could use that as an excuse to attack the currency.
